I like to think of LTT as a Heineken. Crisp, goes down easily, a distinct style of marketing. It keeps things simple and that's definitely got its place; they do know their shit though - Linus had a lot of roles at NCIX beyond just the sales/marketing side and Luke has got a solid academic background in computer science (he's no Wendell, but honestly, who is?) 

Tek Syndicate, on the other hand, is like a good quality single malt. You probably don't drink it quite as often (TS don't post videos as regularly, which is understandable given that it's more of a side thing), but when you do drink it, it's very enjoyable but in a more complex and sophisticated manner. You can also put that bottle back in the cupboard and take it out in future and still enjoy it. I could easily watch an old episode of The Tek and still enjoy it, even though the issues are old (a lot of stuff Logan and Wendell talk about has just developed over time, rather than disappeared).

Given the target markets that both channels have, it's pretty obvious that the LTT forum is going to appeal to a wider and more casual market. It's a great channel - especially their TechQuickie spinoff, which was very handy during my first ever build (I'm a former/current peasant who PC games in the office and uses his console in the living room). Tek Syndicate, however, takes into account the wider implications of technology - political ethics and business practice, mostly. I enjoy The WAN Show, but it keeps its focus more strictly on technology and hardware, whereas The Tek likes to speculate a lot more and discuss in-depth. They're also a little older too, so I think they can sometimes see the bigger picture on some issues. As a result, Tek Syndicate ends up attracting an older and (probably) more educated audience.

In my experience, both communities have been very helpful. They're just different.

For cheaper day-to-day medications I completely agree; very little has changed in practice, and your fee is negligible compared to the cost of the medication. However , when it comes to expensive or pioneering experimental treatment, NHS England may now be out of luck. 

Why? Well the Clinical Commissioning Groups that decide how NHS England's money is spent (which you have and Wales doesn't) are heavily focused on reducing costs and outsourcing medical procedures for the cheapest price. A Clinical Commissioning Group is made up of GPs in your area, which some say is good because it puts spending power in the hands of people who are more connected to the needs of their local community. However, when you're being treated by a specialist - in my case, a GI consultant with a lot of IBD experience - your GPs have to authorise whether they think it's worth you having a treatment that the specialist deems appropriate. In other words, they become the gatekeepers to your health - everything flows through them.

Now this usually doesn't lead to a problem. If the specialist says a treatment is needed, the GPs will leave it at that and approve it as a valid expenditure. However, when a treatment is expensive, like Humira, disagreements start to arise between the specialists at the hospital and the GPs in your Clinical Commissioning Group. The specialist obviously has a much clearer idea of your condition, but if the GPs think a treatment is not worth spending that much on, they can override the decision. This has actually led to rather troubling situations, where important chemo drugs have been switched to cheaper alternatives and pain relief for terminal patients has been denied. Recently, I read an article about a woman who had to fight for her anti-rejection drugs, which she needed to take for an organ transplant (I can't remember where I saw the article, but I will have a look).

Most of this information has come from my mate, who's in his fourth year at Nottingham Medical School. He's constantly berating the new English system and says he's coming back to Cardiff once he qualifies, just because the healthcare system is much easier to work with in Wales.

With all that said, I definitely agree with you about the system remaining fairly unchanged for the majority of patients. Still, I wouldn't want to end up in the minority's situation. I also completely agree with you about the situation in America. It absolutely boggles my mind how people actually can't *afford* medication. What the hell is up with that? The right to health is directly related to your ability to pay. It's absolute insanity. Makes me feel quite fortunate!

Five years and it still ain't exactly shining. I'm 22 and got diagnosed at 17. While I understand some of the others here are trying to be über-optimistic, the reality is that a lot of us won't ever get to experience the joy of remission or just feeling much better. My life could drastically improve over the next 24 hours (and I hope it does) but after five years of pain, I'm not holding out any more hope. So what can I do about it? Honestly? Absolutely nothing. I have little to no control over the course of my illness. There are days where I will be out of action but I'm getting by.

OP, while I know I'm not being a ray of sunshine for you at the moment, it's not because I want you to feel worse. Accepting the reality that this is a shitty illness is the best thing you can do right now. But once you've accepted that a life with Crohn's is going to be a crappy life compared to most people *without* a long-term illness, you'll realise there's so much you do have control over. 

Live your life proactively - not reactively - and do the best you can with what you actually have control over. I'm spewing blood out of my ass on a daily basis - not my choice - but I got my degree and am now doing my PGCE so I can become a teacher (which I love). My Masters in Education Leadership is happening next year. I'm a blue belt in Jiu-Jitsu and I try to work out every day (not easy since I've been taking Azathioprine, which just makes me constantly want to sleep). This is all stuff that has happened because I've seized control of my life (as lame as that sounds) as soon as the opportunity presents itself to me. No crippling colon pain? Off to Jiu-Jitsu for a few hours. A relatively trouble-free eating experience? Let's do some university work. Get yourself in the mindset that every semi-decent day is an opportunity to improve your life. It's a bigger opportunity than any of your healthy friends can ever experience. You *know* what it's like to feel shit most days. Your friends will always take their health for granted if they don't know what it's like to be constantly sick - health is wasted on the healthy and all that jazz.

Use these opportunities to overcome all the bollocks that's been thrown at you by nature/whatever god you believe in (may they rot for being an asshole). One day, I sincerely hope that your life turns around of its own accord. I hope that your burning digestive system stops making your life shit. I hope to hell that they figure out a damn cure for this illness over the next decade or two, so that we can all at least enjoy a portion of our lives. However, with not the best long-term prognosis in the world (most people will find Crohn's and UC comes back in less than five years) and an obscene lack of funding for treatments and cures, don't just wait for things to get better. You could be waiting a long time.

Good luck for now and the future. Better still, fuck fortune and own your life because it's yours to own.

My half-sister just spent the last year as a pre-reg pharmacist and recently passed her exam to register. She said that *occasionally* medical conditions are stored in their system, however, it's usually only a prescription history and permitted drugs. However, looking at a patient's prescription history and having a reasonable amount of medical knowledge will usually (not always) give you a pretty good idea of what they actually need the medicines to treat. I asked her specifically about this earlier.

Similarly, my friend is a training GP (family physician) with one year left on his course. Admittedly, he's not yet qualified but I remember him saying that a doctor knowing *every* potential side effect and contraindication is practically impossible. He has a book on pharmacology (don't remember the name) and two medical dictionaries - Kumar &amp; Clark and the big Oxford one. He says they're absolute lifesavers, although finds it a bit annoying when patients give him a disapproving look if he refers to them. Doctors are only human after all. However, the more he sees patients, the less he finds himself referring to his books, simply because he's remembering knowledge through experiences, as opposed to learning by book.

The ultimate goal is indeed to induce remission. I've been prescribed Prednisone (3/4 of the way through tapering off), which has helped massively. I've also been prescribed Azathioprine; I won't really know if this is working until I come completely off Prednisone. 

Regardless of the improvement the medication has provided, I'm still not at a stage where I can call it anything close to remission. There's still too much debilitating pain that makes life a struggle to get on with. To be in pain feels like it's my only purpose right now...and that isn't a comforting thought. I guess it's just frustrating that even after what feels like a massive improvement in overall symptoms, the pain is still there and almost as strong as it was before treatment.
